title: Cover-sheet memo
start: A single report about the size of a paperback lies squared on a pale neutral tabletop, a thick stack of ivory paper with crisp edges held by a brushed graphite binder clip. Its top sheet is plain where a cover sheet should be, and one small folded memo is clipped to its corner, the crease sharp. To the left, a graphite pneumatic tube terminal the height of a mug stands with its frosted acrylic canister docked. Behind the report sits an empty graphite in-tray, and to the right a small graphite pin rail holds a single blank card. The one acid-lime element is the tab of an unmarked cover sheet resting apart on the in-tray, the piece the report is actually missing. Faint paper dust lines the stack's edge.
end: The same report is almost gone under memos. Identical folded ivory memos burst from the mouth of the pneumatic terminal, which has spat its frosted canister onto its side, and a fan of memos is frozen mid-flight between the tube and the report. The in-tray has overflowed and slid forward, tipping a cascade of memos across the tabletop, and the pin rail sags with cards pinned three deep. Every memo lands on the report pile, clipped and overlapping, bowing the binder clip open. The lime cover-sheet tab is pinned flat beneath the drift at its left edge, barely showing. Creased corners, scuffed folds, a fine haze of paper fibre and a trail of memos lead straight back to the tube.
apocalypse: A wide miniature snowfield of layered ivory memos stretches to a pale horizon, its folds packed into ridges and crevasses like old glacier ice. Rising from it are the bleached tops of cubicle partitions in a long broken row, their graphite frames bent and half buried. In the foreground the pneumatic tube terminal, now the size of a silo, lies snapped at its base, its frosted canister cracked open and choked with fibre. Beyond it, a slim graphite gantry on four thin legs straddles a hollow where the original report lies exposed, its pages swollen and curled. The gantry's acid-lime clamping jaws are lowering one clean cover sheet squarely onto it, while a graphite survey stake marks the cleared hollow.

title: Exiled stapler
start: A heavy desk stapler about the length of a pencil rests on an ivory card blotter at the front of a pale neutral tabletop. Its upper arm is acid-lime enamel, the one lime element, over a brushed graphite base with a visible hinge pin. A crisp, pencil-thin graphite outline traced on the blotter marks its proper spot exactly. Behind it, a row of three miniature graphite desks recedes toward the back of the table, and on the right a narrow frosted acrylic stairwell model steps down out of frame. A folded ivory jacket hangs over the nearest desk chair, left by someone gone to lunch. Fine eraser crumbs and a few stray staples sit on the blotter, and dust softens the outline's edge.
end: The outline on the blotter is now empty, and the lime stapler has been pushed away across the whole layout. A skid trail of scuffed graphite marks and scattered staples runs from the outline past each desk, where boxes of papers have been dumped to fill its place. The stapler is frozen mid-tumble at the top of the frosted stairwell, tilted nose-down over the first step, its arm flipped open and a spray of loose staples hanging in the air below it. At the foot of the stairs, a dim graphite storage shelf is crammed with other displaced desk objects, a graphite tape dispenser and a frosted glass mug among them. The ivory jacket has slid off its chair onto the floor.
apocalypse: A flooded basement ruin spreads wide and low, still grey water reaching to a far row of cracked frosted-glass block pillars fading into haze. Islands of rubble break the surface: a toppled graphite storage shelf the size of a building, a sunken frosted mug, drifts of soggy ivory boxes slumping into the water. Snapped desk frames stand in lines like old piers. Near the centre, on a raised graphite landing, the old stapler sits weathered and pale, its paint worn back to bare metal. A slim graphite lift mast rises from the landing up through a broken slab toward a shaft of daylight, and its acid-lime platform has just cradled the stapler and begun to climb, water dripping from its underside.

title: Printer taken to the field
hero: jammed desk printer on a cart
start: A compact desk printer about the size of a shoebox stands on a slim graphite cart with four small castors at the centre of a pale neutral tabletop. Its casing is matte graphite with chamfered corners and a frosted acrylic output tray. A single ivory sheet is jammed half out of the feed slot, crumpled into an accordion. The one acid-lime element is the small status lamp on the top panel, glowing to flag the jam. Behind the cart, a strip of pale ivory card runs to the back edge as a miniature pathway, and at the far right a patch of ivory paper grass, cut into thin fringed strips, marks an open field. Grey toner dust coats the tray lip, and the castors show faint scuffs.
end: The same cart has rolled along the ivory pathway and stopped at the edge of the paper-grass field, one castor snagged in the fringe and the cart pitching forward. The printer has slid off and landed on its side in the grass, lid sprung open, its frosted output tray snapped and lying a short span away. The jammed sheet has finally torn free and hangs frozen in the air above it, with a burst of loose ivory pages from the feeder fanning back toward the pathway. A cloud of grey toner dust hangs over the impact point, and small graphite screws and a roller spring lie scattered in an arc. The lime status lamp still glows from the upturned panel.
apocalypse: A wide overgrown meadow of ivory paper grass rolls toward low hills on the horizon, scorched grey in broad patches. Printer fragments lie scattered across it at building scale: a cracked graphite side panel standing upright like a wall, a split frosted tray bleached white, snapped rollers half sunk in the ground like fallen columns. Torn pages have weathered into pale sediment between the tufts. In the midground, a slim graphite rail sled runs on two thin tracks between a set of rebuilt feed rollers, and its acid-lime guide rollers are threading one clean sheet from a restored input tray through to a new frosted output tray, a single complete paper path running straight across the ruin.

title: Flair quota
hero: lanyard strap loaded with pin badges
start: An ivory paper lanyard strap about the length of a forearm hangs from a slim brushed graphite hook stand at the centre of a pale neutral tabletop, its clip resting on a blank ivory badge card. Three small round pin badges are fixed to the strap, each a plain graphite disc with a milled edge and no design. Beside the stand, a shallow frosted acrylic dish holds a supply of spare blank pins. The one acid-lime element is a thin marker on a graphite gauge bar at the stand's base, set at the minimum number of pins expected. To the left, a folded ivory card work shirt lies flat and crisp. Fine lint and a few loose pin backs rest on the tabletop.
end: The same lanyard strap is now fully armoured in pins, badges overlapping like scales from hook to clip. More have spread onto the folded ivory shirt, which has been dragged against the stand and sags under rows of graphite discs pinned into collar, cuffs and pocket, the card puckering around each one. The weight has bent the graphite hook into a curve, and the whole stand is tipping to the right, frozen mid-fall. The frosted dish has been knocked over, and a shower of pins is caught spilling across the tabletop, some bouncing, some rolling. The lime gauge marker is still visible at the base, but it has been pushed up to a higher notch. Scratches and pin backs litter the surface.
apocalypse: A wide grey shingle beach of loose graphite pin badges stretches to a flat horizon, countless discs layered in shallow terraces and wind-sorted by size. Half sunk in the shingle lie the ruins of the hook stand, now the height of a radio mast, bent double and flaking. Long strips of the ivory shirt are buried in ridges, pierced and frayed, bleached almost white. Pin backs collect in small drifts in the hollows. In the midground, a slim graphite crane on a tracked base swings its boom over the shingle, its acid-lime electromagnet plate lowered just above the surface as a cluster of pins leaps upward to meet it. Beneath the boom sits one small frosted acrylic tray holding a neat single layer of pins.

title: Saturday request
hero: weekend desk calendar with request slip
start: A desk calendar about the width of a laptop sits in the middle of a pale neutral tabletop, a brushed graphite easel holding a crisp ivory card grid of blank squares. The two squares at the right end of each row are the weekend, a slightly paler ivory. On the first weekend, a single acid-lime sticky request slip is pressed onto the Saturday square, its top edge curling. In front of the calendar lies a folded ivory card jacket on a graphite hanger, left behind on a Friday evening, and to the left a graphite pad dispenser holds a neat stack of blank ivory slips. Fine fibres show at the grid's perforated edge, and a thin line of dust catches along the slip's adhesive strip.
end: The same calendar now bristles with request slips. Ivory slips from the graphite dispenser have spread from Saturday to Sunday, then down the right columns across every weekend below, layered three and four deep until no rest day is visible. Their curled edges lift like feathers, and several are frozen mid-air, peeling off the stack, while the dispenser has tipped forward and is spitting slips onto the tabletop. The weight has bowed the ivory card grid and pulled the graphite easel into a lean. The original acid-lime slip is still on the first Saturday, buried at the bottom of the layers with one corner showing. The jacket has slipped from its hanger and lies half under the fallen pile.
apocalypse: A quiet miniature town of low ivory card houses lies in a wide valley, seen from a hillside, its streets fading toward a pale horizon. Across the valley floor lies the vast fallen calendar grid, cracked into tiles that rest on rooftops and in yards like terraced fields, the squares weathered grey and split. Drifts of old request slips have settled over everything like leaf litter, banked against every wall. The graphite easel stands snapped in the distance like a broken pylon. In the foreground, a slim graphite roller rig on two rails is pressing slips aside from two adjacent weekend squares, and a pair of graphite survey stakes strung with taut acid-lime cord fence those two squares off, swept clean.

title: Lane-switch commute
hero: two-lane highway model with lane-switching car
start: A miniature two-lane highway section about the length of a forearm runs diagonally across a pale neutral tabletop, its road surface matte graphite with ivory paper lane dashes and chamfered graphite kerbs. Small graphite car models, each the size of a matchbox, sit bumper to bumper in both lanes, their windows sandblasted frosted glass so the cabins read as empty. One car in the right lane is angled halfway across the dash line, caught mid lane change, and its acid-lime roof is the one lime element. The left lane shows a short gap just ahead of it; the right lane is packed. Tiny scuffs, fine road grit and a thin trail of dust behind the switching car show it has just moved.
end: The same highway section is now a frozen jam. The lime-roofed car has switched back and forth, leaving a zigzag of scuff marks across the ivory dashes, and now sits boxed in near the rear of the left lane, which has stopped dead. The right lane it left has started moving: its cars are pulling ahead toward the far end, wheels kicking up thin plumes of dust frozen in the air. Where the car cut across, two models have nudged each other, one rotated sideways over the dash line, one tipped onto two wheels. A kerb section has been knocked loose and is caught mid-fall off the table edge. Fine grit sprays from under the stalled wheels.
apocalypse: A long cracked highway viaduct crosses a wide dry canyon of layered ivory paper strata, receding to a hazy horizon. Its graphite deck is split into slabs, some tilted, some fallen into the canyon, and the kerbs are bleached and crumbling. Car models the size of houses sit stalled in both lanes, frosted windows crazed with cracks and roofs drifted with pale dust. One lies on its side at the edge of a broken span. Straddling the deck, a slim graphite bridge-laying rig on thin spindly legs is lowering fresh graphite slabs into the gap between the stalled lanes, and its acid-lime alignment rails mark out a clear new third lane running down the exact middle toward the far end.

title: Desk to storage B
hero: window cubicle pushed toward the boiler
start: A single miniature cubicle about the size of a shoebox sits at the left of a pale neutral tabletop beside a tall frosted acrylic window panel that glows softly. Its walls are ivory card partitions on graphite posts, with a small graphite desk, a jacket folded over the tucked-in chair and a blank ivory nameplate on the entrance post. The one acid-lime element is the shade of the small desk lamp. To the right, the tabletop steps down through a series of graphite floor plates, each lower and darker, toward a boiler model of brushed graphite pipes and a riveted drum at the far right edge. A thin line of dust along the partition tops shows the cubicle has stood here a long while.
end: The same cubicle has been moved, and moved again. Its old spot by the frosted window is marked only by four dust-free squares where the posts stood. Along the descending graphite floor plates, the partitions have been cut down in stages, with trimmed ivory card offcuts left curled on each step. The cubicle now sits jammed against the boiler at the far right, squeezed to half its width, one partition buckled against a pipe, the chair wedged sideways under the desk. The lime-shaded lamp is tipping off the desk edge, frozen mid-fall, its cord trailing. The jacket has slid onto the floor plate, and a puff of soot and dust hangs where the drum presses into the partition.
apocalypse: A wide underground cavern of fallen ceiling slabs stretches back into darkness, with distant rubble slopes as the only depth cue. Graphite pipes the size of tunnels lie cracked across the floor, and the boiler drum sits split and dull at the centre like a collapsed dome. Half buried in rubble at its base is the cubicle, its ivory partitions crushed, delaminated and mottled, the nameplate snapped off. Old card offcuts have compacted into pale sediment layers in the debris. From beside the cubicle, a slim telescopic graphite mast has pushed straight up through a breach in the ceiling slabs, and the acid-lime reflector at its top catches daylight and throws a single clean beam down onto the cubicle desk.

title: Efficiency consultants
start: A small interview table of brushed graphite, about the width of a hardback book, stands at the centre of a pale neutral tabletop. On one side, two empty graphite chairs sit side by side; facing them across the table is a single chair, its ivory seat pad still dented. On the table lies a graphite clipboard holding an ivory audit form of blank tick boxes, a pen resting across it. The one acid-lime element is an unmarked removal tag on a thin thread, lying beside the clipboard, ready to be used. Behind the table, four miniature graphite desks stand in a neat row, each with a cold frosted mug or a folded jacket left on it. Eraser crumbs and pencil dust mark the form.
end: The same interview table now carries a teetering stack of ivory audit forms, clipboard after clipboard piled until the stack leans and sheets slide off its left side, frozen in a fan across the tabletop. The single chair has been pushed back and tipped onto two legs. Behind, every desk in the row now wears an ivory card tag on thread, and the first desk has been dragged out of line, its mug toppled and rolling, its jacket half off. The original lime tag hangs from the second desk, twisting on its thread. Loose forms have slid into the gaps between desks, marking a trail from the table to each one. Scuffed drag marks and paper dust follow the moved desk.
apocalypse: A wide flat plain of compacted ivory audit forms stretches to a hazy horizon, the sheets cracked and layered like dry mudflats. Across it stand long uneven rows of abandoned graphite desks, now the size of houses, like a field of markers, many tipped or sunk to their drawers, each with a bleached, frayed tag still hanging from it. The interview table lies overturned in the foreground, one leg snapped. In the midground, a slim graphite gantry sorter rides on two long rails above the rows, and its acid-lime grab is lifting one sound desk clear of the forms and setting it onto a flat graphite conveyor that carries a short line of restored desks toward a rebuilt, evenly spaced row.

title: Insomnia copier
start: A desktop copier about the size of a small suitcase sits at the left of a pale neutral tabletop, matte graphite with chamfered edges, its sandblasted frosted glass lid slightly raised over the original. A single crisp ivory copy lies in the frosted acrylic output tray, sharp-edged, its blank layout of blocks and ruled lines matching the original exactly. The one acid-lime element is the copier's round start key on the top panel. To the right, an empty graphite in-tray waits, and a cold frosted glass mug with a dried ring sits near the table edge, left from a long evening. Faint toner dust shows along the tray lip. Soft grey light suggests the very small hours of the night.
end: The same copier is running flat out. Its lid is propped open with a copy on the glass instead of the original, and each copy feeds out a little greyer and grainier than the last, the blocks and lines smudging into mottled speckle. Copies stream from the tray in a continuous arc, frozen mid-air, landing in a sliding stack that has overflowed the in-tray and spread across the tabletop toward the mug, which is tipping over the edge. The lime start key is held down under a wedged graphite ruler. The original ivory sheet lies trapped beneath the pile with one corner showing. A warm toner haze drifts above the copier, and fine grey powder coats everything downstream.
apocalypse: A wide dune sea of grey copies rolls away under dim night light to a flat horizon, each dune built from countless faded, grainy sheets packed into drifts, their surfaces rippled by wind. Near the foreground the copier rises from a dune, now the size of a warehouse, its frosted lid snapped off, its glass cracked and silted with toner. The fallen mug lies rim-up in a hollow, filled with grey powder. In the midground, a slim graphite scanning bridge on two thin legs spans a trough between dunes, its acid-lime light bar sweeping slowly along the sheets below. At the bridge's end, a jointed graphite arm lifts one crisp, bright ivory original clear of the grey drift.

title: Catalogue apartment
hero: flat-pack furniture carton in a studio room
start: A single flat-pack furniture carton about the size of a shoebox sits on the floor of a miniature studio room set on a pale neutral tabletop. The room is three ivory card walls with a frosted acrylic window in the back one. The carton is crisp ivory corrugated card with blank sides and a taped seam. On top of it lies an office ID badge, a plain graphite rectangle on an acid-lime lanyard, the one lime element. A small graphite hex key rests beside it. The rest of the room is nearly bare: one frosted glass lamp in the corner and one folded blanket against the wall. Fibres fray at the carton's torn corner, and floor dust gathers in the room's edges.
end: The same studio room is now packed with identical flat-pack furniture. Carton after carton has been opened and assembled: matching ivory card shelves, matching graphite side tables, matching frosted lamps, the same models repeated in rows until the room reads as a showroom display. Empty cartons are stacked against the window, blocking its glow, and a tower of them leans out of the room's open side, frozen mid-topple, its top carton sliding off. Spare hex keys and packing scraps litter the floor. The office badge has slipped down between two cartons, with only a loop of the lime lanyard still showing. The blanket is crushed under a table leg. Torn card and fibre dust drift in the air.
apocalypse: A wide collapsed showroom stretches to a hazy far wall, fallen flat-pack panels stacked in tilted strata like shale cliffs, the ivory card faded and the graphite frames bent. Repeated identical tables and shelves protrude from the slopes, bleached and delaminating, and snapped frosted lamps lie in rows like fallen posts. Through the middle of this terrain, a slim graphite plough rig on low tracks is pushing a clean corridor, its acid-lime blade angled to shove panels aside into neat banks. The corridor leads to one small cleared room at the centre: three ivory walls, a glowing frosted window, a single worn blanket and a cold mug on the floor, lived in and uncluttered.

title: Single-serving travel
hero: seatback tray table with single-portion items
start: A fold-down tray table about the size of a hardback, brushed graphite with a chamfered latch, sits level at the centre of a pale neutral tabletop against the back of a matte graphite seat model. On it rest a single ivory card meal box with a crisp folded lid, a tiny frosted acrylic soap cube, a sealed portion-sized ivory packet and a torn boarding stub of blank ivory card. The one acid-lime element is the small latch knob on the seatback, turned to hold the tray. In the seat pocket sit a folded ivory blanket and an empty frosted cup. Crumbs, a hairline scuff across the tray and loose fibres along the stub's torn edge complete the scene.
end: The same tray table is overflowing with single-portion packages. Trip after trip has added more: dozens of tiny meal boxes, soap cubes, sealed packets and folded blankets are heaped in a mound far wider than the tray, sliding off every side. The tray has dropped on its hinge under the weight and tilts forward, and a cascade of soap cubes and packets is frozen mid-fall toward the tabletop, some bouncing where they land. Boarding stubs caught in the mound flutter at its edges. The lime latch knob has been forced round by the tilting tray. The seat pocket is bursting, split along its seam. Crumbs and ivory fibres hang in the air above the pile.
apocalypse: A wide landfill of tiny single-portion packages rolls to a hazy horizon in low mounds and terraces, meal boxes crushed flat, soap cubes weathered into frosted pebbles, blankets bleached and matted into the layers. Winding through it is the ruin of a baggage conveyor the size of a railway, its graphite belt torn and its rollers dull and snapped. The seatback and tray table stand tipped upright in the middle distance like a broken monument. In the foreground, a slim graphite compactor rig on four jointed legs works a patch of the heap, its acid-lime press plate descending to square a mixed pile into a tidy bale. Beside it, a short row of finished bales sits sorted by type.

title: Recall formula
hero: balance scale weighing a car against claim forms
start: A graphite balance scale about the height of a table lamp stands at the centre of a pale neutral tabletop, its beam brushed graphite with a chamfered pivot and two shallow frosted glass pans on thin rods. On the left pan sits a small graphite car model with a hairline crack along one wheel arch. On the right pan rests a thin stack of blank ivory claim forms, edges crisp. The beam hangs level. The one acid-lime element is the calibration screw at the pivot. Behind the scale, a short queue of three identical car models waits on a graphite plate, bonnets aligned. A few fine metal filings lie under the cracked wheel arch, and dust softens the pans' rims.
end: The same scale has been loaded and adjusted again and again. Claim forms keep landing on the right pan in a fanned pile, some frozen mid-drop above it, and the pile has forced that pan hard down. Instead of repairing the cracked car, the lime calibration screw has been cranked far out, its thread exposed, and a graphite counterweight clipped to the car side drags the beam back toward level. The queue of cars has grown into a long line snaking back to the table edge, bonnet to bumper, the last one tipping off. The crack in the first car has spread across its door. Forms have slid from the pan into drifts around the base.
apocalypse: A wide scrapyard stretches to a low grey horizon, terraced with heaps of car models the size of houses, crushed and dulled, bonnets gaping, frosted windows crazed. Between the heaps, compacted drifts of weathered claim forms have become banks of pale sediment. At the centre, the balance scale stands broken: its pivot tower cracked, the beam fallen with one end buried in forms and the other resting on a flattened car, one frosted pan split. A slim graphite lever crane has set up beside the tower, its long arm prising the beam upward, while an acid-lime fulcrum wedge slides into the cracked pivot to re-seat the beam level for the first time in years.

title: Drive-thru downshift
start: A slim briefcase about the size of a paperback, matte graphite with brushed metal clasps, leans against the side of a miniature drive-thru kiosk on a pale neutral tabletop. The kiosk is ivory card with a small sandblasted frosted glass service window and a graphite awning. Beside the briefcase lies a folded ivory paper headset. A curved graphite lane loops around the kiosk, with one small graphite car model waiting at the window. The one acid-lime element is the small call lamp above the service window, lit for the next order. A single blank ivory order slip rests on the window sill. Dust has settled on the briefcase clasp, and faint tyre scuffs mark the lane.
end: The same kiosk is overwhelmed. The briefcase has been knocked flat and shoved aside against the lane edge, its clasp sprung, while the paper headset has been unfolded and propped on the sill. Blank ivory order slips pour out of the frosted service window in a stream, frozen mid-air, piling on the sill before spilling onto the lane. Behind the first car, a queue of identical graphite car models wraps all the way around the kiosk, bumper to bumper, until the last car noses into the first. The lime call lamp above the window stays lit. Slips have caught under wheels and in the gaps between cars, and a fine haze of paper dust hangs over the lane.
apocalypse: A wide empty drive-thru lot at dusk stretches to a flat horizon, its graphite surface split by long cracks with pale paper weeds pushing through. The kiosk stands roofless in the middle distance, ivory walls bleached and caved in, its frosted window a cracked hole. The looped lane is still visible, ringed by stalled car models the size of houses, sunk to their axles in drifts of weathered order slips. The briefcase lies split open at the lot's edge. In the foreground, a slim graphite line-painting cart on three thin wheels has broken the loop, laying a fresh acid-lime lane marking that peels away from the kiosk and runs straight out across open ground toward the horizon.

title: Two lines lit
start: A desk phone about the size of a hardback sits squared at the centre of a pale neutral tabletop, matte graphite with a chamfered body, a coiled cord and its handset resting in the cradle. On its front are two frosted acrylic line buttons; the left one glows acid-lime, the one lime element, while the right one is dark. Beside the phone lie an ivory notepad with a blank top sheet and a graphite pen, and to the right stands a closed rotary card file of blank ivory cards. Behind the phone, a frosted glass mug of cold coffee sits next to a chair with a jacket over its back. Fine dust lines the button gaps, and one crease crosses the notepad.
end: The same desk is now covered in phones. The right line on the original phone has lit, and behind it extension phones have been stacked into a leaning tower, every frosted line button glowing warm white. Every handset is off its cradle: they dangle on stretched coiled cords, hang over the desk edge, and one is frozen mid-fall toward the floor. The cords drag across the notepad, pulling it off the desk with sheets fanning out. The rotary card file has spun open, blank cards flying loose. The original lime button still glows at the bottom of the stack. The mug has tipped, and a splash of cold coffee is frozen leaving its rim.
apocalypse: A wide quiet field of tall ivory paper grass stretches to a low horizon, and scattered through it lie thousands of dead graphite handsets, their cords coiled in the grass like dry vines, frosted buttons cracked and dark. In the midground stands the collapsed switchboard, a graphite tower the size of a building, its front panel peeled back and its sockets clogged with dust. Rows of snapped graphite poles lead off into the distance. In the foreground, a slim graphite pole-line rig on a tracked base is stringing a single taut acid-lime wire from the switchboard across the field to one handset set upright in a small graphite cradle, re-seated and ready to ring.

title: Locked leads
start: A small graphite filing drawer about the size of a shoebox sits at the centre of a desk model on a pale neutral tabletop, its front brushed metal with a chamfered handle and a keyhole lock. The drawer is shut, and through a slim frosted glass viewing slot in its side a row of blank ivory index cards shows, crisp and tabbed. Beside it, a graphite desk phone sits cold, its handset in the cradle. The one acid-lime element is the small key, hanging out of reach on a hook atop a graphite post at the back of the desk. Beads of water run down a frosted glass window panel behind, and a folded jacket with rain spots lies over the chair.
end: The same locked drawer now holds up the whole room. Around it, other desk models have been dragged in close, each with its own graphite phone, and the phones are piling up untouched, stacked two and three high, receivers in cradles, cords coiled. A graphite pry bar jammed into the drawer seam has bent and is frozen mid-slip, and the lock plate shows fresh gouges. Index-card tabs press against the frosted slot. The lime key still hangs on its hook behind, swinging slightly. Rainwater from the window has run across the tabletop and pooled around the phone stacks, soaking the jacket and the edges of a scattered pack of empty cards. Grit clings to every wet surface.
apocalypse: A wide grey ruin under steady rain stretches to a misted horizon, broken desk frames rising from shallow flooded terraces, the puddles pocked with raindrops. Heaps of graphite phones the size of vans lie drowned and silted in the water. At the centre stands the drawer, now a vault-sized block of pitted graphite, its seam still sealed, the bent pry bar fused into its side, its frosted slot clouded. The hook post has fallen across it. In the foreground, a slim graphite arm rig on a narrow jointed base reaches into the lock, and its acid-lime key is caught mid-turn, the drawer front just beginning to slide open to reveal a sliver of dry ivory index cards inside.

title: Sales leaderboard
start: A wall-mounted leaderboard panel about the size of a tea tray stands upright at the back of a pale neutral tabletop, a brushed graphite frame fixed with four screws to an ivory card wall. Inside it, six slim vertical bars rise from a common baseline to slightly different heights, all matte graphite except one acid-lime bar, the one lime element, just a little ahead of the others. Plain tick marks run up the side rail. In front of the board, a row of three miniature graphite desks points toward it, each with a cold frosted mug and a desk phone. Fine dust gathers on the frame's lower rail, and the wall card shows a faint grain behind the bars.
end: The same leaderboard is being torn off the wall. The bars have raced each other upward, overshooting the frame and jamming against the ivory card ceiling, where they bend and buckle. The lime bar leads, bent almost double at the top. The pressure has popped two of the four mounting screws, which are frozen mid-air, and the frame is peeling away from the wall at its top corners, ripping strips of ivory card with it. Card dust and flakes rain down onto the desks below, where one mug has tipped and a phone is sliding over the edge. The tick marks on the side rail have been left far behind. Scrape marks on the ceiling trace each bar's climb.
apocalypse: A wide ruined sales floor stretches to a dim far wall, the ivory card ceiling long gone and open to pale sky. Across the floor lie the fallen leaderboard bars, now as long as trains, bent and crossed over one another like a log jam, their graphite surfaces flaking. The empty frame hangs twisted from one remaining post. Desks are half buried in drifts of ceiling card and dust. In the midground, a slim graphite gantry on wheeled rails lifts one straightened bar and lowers it beside several others already laid parallel on the floor, while its acid-lime level gauge, a long spirit rail along the gantry beam, checks that every bar sits at exactly the same height.

title: Locked coffee
hero: coffee pot in a locked cabinet
start: A small wall cabinet about the size of a microwave hangs at the back of a pale neutral tabletop, its body brushed graphite, its door a pane of sandblasted frosted glass in a slim graphite frame. Behind the glass a round glass coffee pot sits full on a warming plate, a faint haze of steam against the frosted pane. The one acid-lime element is the small padlock on the door hasp, shut tight. In front of the cabinet, a single empty frosted glass mug waits on the tabletop, a brown ring dried inside it, and a graphite spoon lies beside it on a folded ivory napkin. Fine dust sits on the hasp, and faint smudges dull the graphite handle.
end: The same cabinet stays locked while mugs pile up in front of it. Row after row of empty frosted glass mugs stand queued across the tabletop, handles aligned, the rows stretching back out of frame to the right. The front rows have been pressed against the cabinet base and are stacking two high, and one mug on top is frozen mid-slide, tipping off. The lime padlock hangs untouched on the hasp. Inside, the pot has boiled down to a dark crust, and its steam has fogged the frosted glass. The graphite spoon has been jammed into the hasp and bent. Dried drips run down the glass, and brown rings stain the tabletop under the front mugs.
apocalypse: A wide dry basin stretches to a hazy ridge on the horizon, its floor a cracked crust of pale ivory silt scattered with mug shards like frosted gravel, broken handles poking up in rows where the queues once stood. At the basin's edge stands the cabinet, now the size of a house, its graphite body pitted and its frosted door smashed open, the old padlock dulled to grey. Inside, the pot sits dry and cracked on its plate. A slim graphite pipe stand has been run across the basin from the far ridge on thin legs, and at its end an acid-lime tap valve is turned open, a thin clear stream of coffee just beginning to fall into the empty pot.

title: Fluorescent hum
start: A long corridor model about the length of a forearm runs straight away from the camera across a pale neutral tabletop, its walls ivory card, its floor matte graphite panels, its ceiling a row of slim frosted acrylic light tubes in graphite housings. The fixtures give a flat, even glow, except one near the middle whose tube has dipped dim mid-flicker. The one acid-lime element is the small exit door at the far end, standing slightly ajar. A graphite chair sits against the left wall with a folded jacket on it, and a frosted glass mug stands on the floor beside it. Fine dust lies along the skirting and inside the tube housings.
end: The same corridor has gone grey. The flicker has passed from fixture to fixture down its whole length, every tube stuck at a different brightness, and three have dropped from their housings: one hangs by a single clip, one is frozen mid-fall, and one has shattered on the floor in a spray of frosted fragments. The corridor looks longer than before, its far end lost in dim haze, and the lime exit door has shrunk to a small speck of colour. Dust shaken loose from the housings hangs in the air beneath each fixture. The chair has been pushed out by falling glass, and the mug is rolling on its side across the graphite floor.
apocalypse: A long, dim tunnel ruin stretches deep into darkness, its ivory walls stained grey and buckled, its ceiling half collapsed into slopes of rubble. Fallen light fixtures the size of railway carriages lie across the floor, their graphite housings bent and their frosted tubes broken into shards ground into the dust. A faint pale haze hangs in the air. In the foreground, a slim graphite rail cart has advanced along a thin track laid over the debris, planting small graphite lamp posts at intervals behind it that light the floor in soft pools. The cart's acid-lime lamp head, raised on a thin boom, throws a strong clean beam ahead along the track toward a far opening where the exit door once stood.

title: Half-height floor
start: An office floor model about the size of a shoebox sits on a pale neutral tabletop, open at the front like a cutaway, with a full-height ivory card storey above and another below. The middle floor has a ceiling at half the normal height, a slab of matte graphite resting on slim posts. Beneath it, a small graphite desk has been cut down to fit, and its chair is folded low. A frosted acrylic filing cabinet stands in the corner, its top grazing the ceiling. The one acid-lime element is a small stepped ceiling-height gauge fixed to the left wall, its marker at the lowest notch. A cold frosted mug sits on the desk, and scuffs on the slab underside show where things have scraped.
end: The same half-height floor is being crushed. The graphite ceiling slab has sagged in the middle, pressing down on everything below. The chair has folded flat with its back snapped. The filing cabinet has tipped against the desk, its drawers popped open and ivory files sliding out, frozen mid-fall. The desk legs have splayed and buckled. The slim ceiling posts are bowing outward, and one has snapped and kicked sideways. The storeys above and below stay square and untouched. The lime gauge on the wall is covered by the slab except for its top edge. Fine dust and card fibres puff out along the front edge where the slab grinds against the side walls.
apocalypse: A towering cliff wall of an office building rises above a wide plain of ivory rubble, its upper and lower storeys intact but weathered pale, the horizon fading behind. Between them runs a thin crushed seam, the half-height floor flattened into a compacted layer of graphite, folded furniture and bleached files, like a dark stratum in rock. Rubble slopes fan out below it onto the plain. On a ledge at the base of the seam, a slim graphite jacking rig has inserted a row of thin screw columns into the gap, and their acid-lime jack heads are pushing the ceiling slab upward, opening a clean slot of space above one freed, upright desk and chair.

title: Scripted commute
start: A miniature cul-de-sac about the size of a tea tray sits on a pale neutral tabletop, its road a matte graphite loop around a central ivory card green, lined with five identical ivory card houses with graphite roofs and frosted acrylic windows. Every lawn, fence and mailbox is exactly the same and perfectly aligned. One small graphite car is backing out of a driveway, a tiny graphite briefcase on its roof rack. The one acid-lime element is a single rolled newspaper, blank and unmarked, lying on the doorstep of that house. Beyond the loop, a thin graphite road runs toward the table edge, blocked by a small graphite barrier arm. Fine grit sits along the kerbs.
end: The same cul-de-sac is replaying itself in a tightening loop. The single car has become a line of identical cars circling nose to tail, each with the same briefcase on its roof. The same rolled newspaper lies on every doorstep, and more are frozen mid-air, flung from a graphite chute at the corner toward each step. The loop has pulled inward, its road buckled into a tighter ring that pushes the houses together until their fences overlap and one roof has slid askew. The original lime newspaper is being run over by the circling cars, crushed flat. The barrier on the exit road is still down. Dust and grit spray from the tyres at every bend.
apocalypse: A wide miniature suburb lies weathered and overgrown under a pale sky, seen from a low hill, its streets of identical ivory card houses sagging and roofless as they recede to a flat horizon. At the centre, the cul-de-sac loop is a cracked graphite ring, and a procession of stalled car models the size of buses sits nose to tail around it, roofs drifted with pale dust and bleached newspapers. The barrier on the exit road has seized shut. In the foreground, a slim graphite road-laying rig on thin jointed legs has cut through the ring, and its acid-lime switch plate is set into the road, diverting a newly laid graphite lane off the loop and out past the barrier toward open country.

title: Mailroom deluge
start: A long sorting table of brushed graphite, about the length of a forearm, runs across a pale neutral tabletop at the foot of three frosted acrylic chutes that drop from above. On the table sits a single ivory card parcel tied with fine string, its label blank. Beside it, a slim graphite sorting arm on a pivot hangs poised above a row of open graphite pigeonholes at the back, empty and waiting. The one acid-lime element is the sorting arm's paddle tip. In the foreground, an empty graphite push cart stands with a folded jacket over its handle. The chutes are clean, and the table carries a light dusting of paper fibre and a single stray envelope.
end: The same sorting table is buried. Parcels and envelopes pour from all three frosted chutes at once, a torrent frozen mid-air, overflowing the chute mouths and bouncing off the table in every direction. The table has vanished under a sliding heap that has spilled over its edge and across the tabletop, burying the push cart to its handle. The sorting arm is swung mid-sweep, its lime paddle tip jammed against a parcel it cannot move, the pivot bending. The pigeonholes at the back are stuffed, envelopes jutting from every slot. The original parcel is lost somewhere in the heap. Torn string, crushed corners and a haze of paper dust hang over the pile.
apocalypse: A vast mailroom hall stretches away into shadow, its far wall lost in haze, its floor filled by a parcel landslide that has slumped from three towering chutes into sloping hills. The parcels, now the size of houses, are crushed, bleached and bound in frayed string, with envelopes compacted into pale sediment between them. The graphite pigeonhole wall stands like a cracked honeycomb cliff, choked with paper. The sorting arm lies snapped across the slope. In the midground, a slim graphite sorting rig has cut into the slide and installed a new frosted chute with an acid-lime diverter gate, which feeds parcels one by one into three clean graphite lanes running in parallel across the cleared floor toward the pigeonholes.

title: Called in on a day off
start: A small shopfront model about the size of a toaster sits on a pale neutral tabletop, its front a roller shutter of ribbed brushed graphite slats raised to half height, showing a dim ivory counter inside. To the left of the shutter, pinned to an ivory card board, hangs a calendar page of blank squares, and an acid-lime ring drawn around one square marks the day off, the one lime element. A graphite crank handle sits in its bracket beside the shutter, and a folded jacket and a set of keys rest on the step as if dropped on arrival. A single ivory task slip lies just under the shutter's bottom edge. Fine grit collects in the slat grooves.
end: The same shutter has jammed at half height, its slats buckled on one side where the guide rail has bent, and the crank handle has snapped in its bracket. From underneath, shift tasks pour out onto the pavement: ivory task slips, graphite cash trays and folded ivory boxes, frozen mid-slide as they spill forward. The heap has spread left and is piling against the pinned calendar page, which has torn loose from one pin and is flapping forward, the lime-ringed square half covered by a slip stuck across it. The jacket is buried beneath the pile, and the keys are frozen mid-bounce off the step. Grit shakes loose from the slats in a fine curtain.
apocalypse: A long ruined parade of shops stretches along a cracked street to a vanishing point, every shopfront closed behind dulled graphite shutters, awnings collapsed, ivory walls weathered and stained. Drifts of old task slips and crushed boxes have banked against the shutters like wind-blown sand, and the calendar board lies front down in the street, its card split. Near the foreground, one shutter is still jammed at half height with a heap spilling beneath it. Beside it, a slim graphite winch rig on a braced tripod has hooked its cable to the bottom slat, and its acid-lime crank wheel is mid-turn, the shutter lifting evenly for the first time as a bar of light enters the dim shop behind.

title: Rental drop-box overflow
start: A graphite return drop-box about the size of a small safe stands against an ivory card shop wall on a pale neutral tabletop, its front plate brushed metal with a chamfered hinged slot. A single slim frosted acrylic tape case sits half inserted in the slot, its label blank. To the right, the shop's frosted glass door is closed, with a graphite shelf of neatly spaced cases faintly visible through it. The one acid-lime element is the drop-box's small side flag, raised to show it needs emptying. On the pavement in front lie a few grains of grit and one curled leaf cut from ivory paper. The slot's edges show fine scratches from years of use.
end: The same drop-box has overflowed. Its flap is jammed open and tape cases are bursting out of the slot in a stream, frozen mid-air, while more pile on top of the box and slide off its sides. The pile spills across the pavement in a wide fan toward the camera. Several cases have cracked open on impact, their frosted shells split and ivory tape ribbons unspooling across the ground in loops. The box itself has been shoved forward off its base by the weight and is tilting. The lime flag is bent flat under the heap. Against the frosted door the cases are stacked high, blocking it. Grit, frosted shards and fine dust scatter along the pavement.
apocalypse: A wide drift of tape cases spreads outside a long shuttered store, settled into a sloping moraine that runs toward a pale hazy horizon, the cases bleached, split and packed together like weathered scree, loose tape ribbons flattened into grey streaks across them. The drop-box, now the size of a building, lies tilted and half buried, its flap torn away. The frosted store door is cracked and blocked. In the midground, a slim graphite conveyor on thin trestles runs from the drift up through a cleared doorway into the store, its acid-lime sorting rollers turning cases upright one by one and sliding them onto freshly rebuilt graphite shelves inside, arranged in tidy rows.

title: Impossible sweetener
hero: coffee cup and the one correct sweetener packet
start: A single frosted glass coffee cup on a matching saucer sits at the centre of a pale neutral tabletop, the coffee dark and still, a graphite spoon resting on the saucer. Beside it lies one small sweetener packet, a crisp ivory paper sachet folded at both ends, and its acid-lime tear strip is the one lime element, marking the exact kind that was asked for. Behind the cup, a graphite caddy holds a neat row of ivory packets in several subtly different sizes and folds. To the right, an empty graphite tray waits to carry the cup away. Fine sugar grains dust the saucer rim, and the packets show crisp fibres at their folds.
end: The same desk is now lined with cups. Coffee after coffee has been made and sent back: frosted cups on saucers stretch in a crooked line along the tabletop, each with a torn wrong packet lying beside it. The caddy has been upended, and packets of every size and fold spill from it in a frozen cascade, some mid-air, some sliding across the tray, which has tipped and dumped its cup. A spoon is frozen mid-bounce, and a splash of coffee arcs out of the falling cup. Sugar granules spray across the table. The one packet with the lime tear strip has slid beneath the original saucer, hidden except for a thin sliver of lime.
apocalypse: A wide dry flat of crusted sugar stretches to a low horizon, glinting grey-white and cracked into plates. Across it lie spilled cups the size of water towers, tipped on their sides, their frosted glass crazed and stained, saucers split and half sunk. Drifts of faded ivory packets gather in the lee of each cup, torn and bleached, some fused into the crust. The toppled caddy lies across the middle distance like a fallen building. In the foreground, a slim graphite picker rig on long thin legs sorts through a drift with fine pointed tongs and has just set one intact packet of the right kind into its acid-lime receiving tray, held up on a slender arm above the ruins.

title: Late-night book delivery
hero: bound mock-up book at the foot of a staircase
start: A bound mock-up book about the size of a thick hardback sits on the bottom step of a townhouse staircase model on a pale neutral tabletop. It has plain ivory card covers, a blank spine and a stitched block of crisp pages, and the one acid-lime element is a single ribbon bookmark hanging from its lower edge. The staircase is ivory card treads on graphite stringers, rising to a closed graphite front door with a frosted glass fanlight glowing faintly above it. Beside the book, a graphite key and a folded coat lie on the step. The scene is lit as late night, a soft glow on the treads. Fine dust and a scuffed corner show on the book.
end: The same staircase has stretched. New ivory card treads have been added again and again, so the stairs now climb far higher and steeper, bending toward the back of the tabletop, the frosted fanlight a small glow at the very top. The book has grown heavier: extra ivory sections are being bound into it, loose pages frozen mid-air as they fly in and slot between the covers, and the spine is splitting. Its weight has cracked the bottom tread, which sags, and the book is sliding off it, tipping backward. The lime ribbon bookmark trails straight up the stairs toward the door. The key is falling through the crack, and dust puffs from the broken tread.
apocalypse: A quiet night street of weathered ivory townhouses stretches away along a hillside, windows dark, toward a faint glow on the horizon. In the foreground, the long staircase has collapsed into a slope of snapped treads and bent graphite stringers, like scree climbing to a doorway far above. The book lies at the bottom, now the size of a house, its covers warped and its swollen pages fanned and bleached, loose sections drifted across the street like fallen leaves. A slim graphite funicular rig has laid a pair of straight rails up the ruined slope, and its acid-lime carriage cradle carries the book halfway up on a levelled platform, toward the graphite front door where the frosted fanlight still glows.
